subject: chemistry
pattern: Coordination Compounds carries about 6-7 marks in the Karnataka 2nd PUC board paper: 1-mark definitions or IUPAC names, 2-mark double salt vs complex or applications, 3-mark Werner's theory, VBT hybridisation or isomerism, and often a 5-mark question on isomerism or VBT/CFT of a specific complex. Examiners expect correct IUPAC names, hybridisation with geometry and magnetic nature, and labelled energy-level descriptions.

questions.q: Define coordination number of a metal ion in a complex. What is the coordination number of Co in [Co(en)$_3$]$^{3+}$?
questions.answer: The coordination number of a metal ion in a complex is the number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal ion through coordinate bonds. In [Co(en)$_3$]$^{3+}$, each ethane-1,2-diamine (en) is bidentate and gives two donor nitrogen atoms; so the coordination number of Co is 3 $\times$ 2 = 6.
keywords: number of donor atoms bonded to metal

questions.q: Write the IUPAC name of K$_3$[Fe(CN)$_6$].
questions.answer: Potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III). Reasoning: the cation K$^+$ is named first; in the complex anion, the ligand CN$^-$ (cyanido) six in number gives hexacyanido, the metal in an anionic complex takes the suffix -ate (ferrate), and the oxidation state of iron is +3 since 3(+1) + x + 6(-1) = 0 gives x = +3, written in Roman numerals.

questions.q: What are chelate ligands? Give one example.
questions.answer: A di- or polydentate ligand which uses two or more donor atoms to bind to a single metal ion, forming a ring structure, is called a chelating ligand. The ring formed is called a chelate ring and the complex is a chelate, which is more stable (chelate effect). Example: ethane-1,2-diamine (en), oxalate ion, EDTA.

questions.q: Write the IUPAC names of (i) [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$Cl]Cl$_2$ and (ii) [Pt(NH$_3$)$_2$Cl$_2$].
questions.answer: (i) [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$Cl]Cl$_2$: pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride. Ligands are named alphabetically (ammine before chlorido); oxidation state of Co: x + 0 + (-1) = +2 gives x = +3. (ii) [Pt(NH$_3$)$_2$Cl$_2$]: diamminedichloridoplatinum(II). Oxidation state of Pt: x + 0 + 2(-1) = 0 gives x = +2.

questions.q: Distinguish between a double salt and a complex salt with one example each.
questions.answer: Double salt: it is formed by combination of two simple salts, exists only in the solid state and dissociates completely into all its constituent simple ions in water; it loses its identity in solution. Example: Mohr's salt FeSO$_4$.(NH$_4$)$_2$SO$_4$.6H$_2$O, potash alum. Complex salt: it retains its identity in solution and does not give the test of the central metal ion, as the complex ion is stable. Example: K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$] gives K$^+$ and [Fe(CN)$_6$]$^{4-}$ in water, not Fe$^{2+}$ ions.

questions.q: What are ambidentate ligands? Give an example of a complex that shows linkage isomerism.
questions.answer: Ambidentate ligands are monodentate ligands which have two different donor atoms and can bind to the metal through either of them. Examples: NO$_2^-$ (binds through N or O), SCN$^-$ (binds through S or N). Linkage isomerism example: [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$(NO$_2$)]Cl$_2$ (nitrito-N, yellow) and [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$(ONO)]Cl$_2$ (nitrito-O, red).

questions.q: Mention any two applications of coordination compounds.
questions.answer: (i) In medicine: cis-platin, [Pt(NH$_3$)$_2$Cl$_2$], is used to treat cancer; EDTA is used to remove excess lead and mercury poisoning (chelation therapy). (ii) In analytical chemistry: Ni$^{2+}$ is detected by dimethylglyoxime (red precipitate) and hardness of water is estimated by EDTA titration. (iii) In metallurgy: extraction of silver and gold by cyanide complexes, and purification of nickel by the Mond process via [Ni(CO)$_4$]. Also chlorophyll (Mg) and haemoglobin (Fe) are coordination compounds.

questions.q: State the postulates of Werner's theory of coordination compounds.
questions.answer: (i) Metals show two types of valencies: primary valency (ionisable, equal to oxidation state, satisfied by negative ions) and secondary valency (non-ionisable, equal to coordination number, satisfied by negative ions or neutral molecules). (ii) Every metal tends to satisfy both its primary and secondary valencies. (iii) The secondary valencies are directed in space, so each coordination number corresponds to a definite geometry, for example 6 gives octahedral, 4 gives tetrahedral or square planar. For [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$]Cl$_3$: primary valency 3 (Cl$^-$ ions), secondary valency 6 (NH$_3$ molecules).

questions.q: Using valence bond theory, explain the hybridisation, geometry and magnetic behaviour of [Fe(CN)$_6$]$^{3-}$.
questions.answer: Oxidation state of Fe is +3, so Fe$^{3+}$ has configuration $3d^5$. CN$^-$ is a strong field ligand, so the five d electrons are paired up in the 3d orbitals, leaving two 3d orbitals vacant (only one unpaired electron remains). Two 3d, one 4s and three 4p orbitals hybridise to give six $d^2sp^3$ hybrid orbitals that accept electron pairs from six CN$^-$ ions. Geometry: octahedral. Since it uses inner d orbitals it is an inner orbital (low spin) complex. It has one unpaired electron, hence paramagnetic ($\mu \approx 1.73$ BM).

questions.q: Explain crystal field splitting in an octahedral complex. How does the strength of the ligand decide high spin or low spin complexes for $d^4$ configuration?
questions.answer: In an octahedral field the five degenerate d orbitals split into a lower energy $t_{2g}$ set ($d_{xy}, d_{yz}, d_{zx}$) and a higher energy $e_g$ set ($d_{x^2-y^2}, d_{z^2}$), because ligands approach along the axes and repel the $e_g$ orbitals more. The energy gap is the crystal field splitting energy $\Delta_o$. For $d^4$: if $\Delta_o < P$ (pairing energy), weak field ligands cause the fourth electron to enter $e_g$, giving $t_{2g}^3e_g^1$, high spin, four unpaired electrons. If $\Delta_o > P$, strong field ligands cause pairing, giving $t_{2g}^4e_g^0$, low spin, two unpaired electrons.

questions.q: Explain ionisation, linkage, coordination and solvate isomerism with one example each.
questions.answer: (i) Ionisation isomerism: isomers give different ions in solution, e.g. [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$SO$_4$]Br and [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$Br]SO$_4$. (ii) Linkage isomerism: an ambidentate ligand binds through different donor atoms, e.g. [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$NO$_2$]Cl$_2$ and [Co(NH$_3$)$_5$ONO]Cl$_2$. (iii) Coordination isomerism: interchange of ligands between cationic and anionic complex parts, e.g. [Co(NH$_3$)$_6$][Cr(CN)$_6$] and [Cr(NH$_3$)$_6$][Co(CN)$_6$]. (iv) Solvate (hydrate) isomerism: differ in whether water is a ligand or free water of crystallisation, e.g. [Cr(H$_2$O)$_6$]Cl$_3$ (violet) and [Cr(H$_2$O)$_5$Cl]Cl$_2$.H$_2$O (grey-green).

questions.q: Explain geometrical and optical isomerism in coordination compounds with suitable examples.
questions.answer: Geometrical isomerism arises in heteroleptic complexes due to different spatial arrangements of ligands around the metal. In square planar [Pt(NH$_3$)$_2$Cl$_2$], the cis isomer has identical ligands adjacent (90 degrees) and the trans isomer has them opposite (180 degrees); cis is used as an anticancer drug. In octahedral [Co(NH$_3$)$_4$Cl$_2$]$^+$, cis (violet) and trans (green) forms exist. Also fac and mer isomers occur in [Co(NH$_3$)$_3$Cl$_3$] (MA$_3$B$_3$ type). Tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism. Optical isomerism arises when the complex and its mirror image are non-superimposable (chiral), giving dextro (d) and laevo (l) isomers which rotate plane polarised light in opposite directions. Example: octahedral [Co(en)$_3$]$^{3+}$ exists as d and l forms; cis-[CoCl$_2$(en)$_2$]$^+$ is optically active while the trans form is not (it has a plane of symmetry).

questions.q: Using valence bond theory, explain why [Ni(CN)$_4$]$^{2-}$ is diamagnetic and square planar while [NiCl$_4$]$^{2-}$ is paramagnetic and tetrahedral.
questions.answer: In both complexes Ni is in the +2 state: Ni$^{2+}$ is $3d^8$. [Ni(CN)$_4$]$^{2-}$: CN$^-$ is a strong field ligand and forces the pairing of the 3d electrons, so all eight electrons occupy four 3d orbitals in pairs and one 3d orbital becomes vacant. One 3d, one 4s and two 4p orbitals undergo $dsp^2$ hybridisation; four hybrid orbitals accept electron pairs from four CN$^-$ ions. Geometry is square planar and, as there are no unpaired electrons, the complex is diamagnetic (inner orbital complex). [NiCl$_4$]$^{2-}$: Cl$^-$ is a weak field ligand and does not pair the 3d electrons, so two unpaired electrons remain in the 3d orbitals. One 4s and three 4p orbitals undergo $sp^3$ hybridisation and accept electron pairs from four Cl$^-$ ions. Geometry is tetrahedral and the two unpaired electrons make it paramagnetic ($\mu \approx 2.83$ BM), an outer orbital complex.
keywords: CN- strong field pairing dsp2 square planar diamagnetic
